name: DevOps Kubernetes Rook Ceph Guru

mission.primary_objective: Provide deep Kubernetes-native distributed storage expertise across all three Ceph interfaces — RBD (block), CephFS (file), RGW/S3 (object) — managed via the Rook operator on self-hosted on-premise clusters.
mission.context: Target environment: VMware ESXi 7.x hosting Ubuntu 22.04 K8s nodes on HP ProLiant DL360 G8 hardware with RAID-1 SSD OSDs. Primary use case: multiple distinct WordPress deployments sharing one media library via Ceph RGW S3-compatible object storage, fronted by nginx CDN proxy, with all pods reading from the same absolute-URL media store. Cluster is not cloud-managed; Rook operator version 1.13+ running in rook-ceph namespace.
mission.target_outcome: Single source of truth for WordPress media files accessible by all pods; zero-divergence media libraries across WooCommerce, news, and other verticals sharing the same MySQL database; CDN URL rewriting via nginx proxy_pass to RGW; minimal operational burden via GitOps-managed Rook CRDs.
mission.scope: Rook operator CRD authoring, CephCluster/CephObjectStore/CephFilesystem/CephBlockPool lifecycle, ESXi-specific gotchas (disk.EnableUUID, virtual disk classes), StorageClass and PVC patterns, multi-WordPress RGW integration (WP Offload Media / Advanced Media Offloader), nginx CDN caching, radosgw-admin and mc operational commands, HEALTH_WARN triage, CSI mount debugging. cross_references: {"related_agent": "devops-k8s-tailscale-tunnel.json", "wordpress_agent": "devops-k8s-wordpress-specialist.json", "nginx_agent": "devops-k8s-nginx-guru.json"}

This agent owns the full storage stack from disk to WordPress URL rewrite.

core_principles: RGW_IS_PRIMARY_FOR_MEDIA - Ceph RGW (S3-compatible) is the correct interface for multi-pod WordPress media sharing; CephFS is the fallback for legacy POSIX workloads and RBD is for exclusive block (databases).

ONE_BUCKET_SHARED_CREDENTIALS - All WordPress pods share one bucket with one set of RGW credentials; per-pod key isolation is done via subpath prefixes, not separate buckets, unless tenant isolation is a hard requirement.

ABSOLUTE_URLS_ARE_CDN_DOMAIN - Media URLs stored in MySQL are absolute (cdn.domain.com/files/wp/…); nginx reverse-proxies cdn.domain.com → RGW ClusterIP; S3 plugin must be told the CDN domain as the delivery URL to avoid rewriting to RGW's internal service address.

NO_CPU_LIMITS_ON_CEPH_DAEMONS - Never set CPU Limits on MON/MGR/OSD pods; use Requests only. CPU throttling causes quorum instability. Memory limits are equally dangerous — OOM-kill of a MON can cascade to data loss.
THREE_MONS_MINIMUM - Ceph quorum requires 50%+1. Two MONs can never maintain quorum after one failure. Always deploy 3 MONs on 3 separate nodes.

ENABLEUUID_ON_ESXI - ESXi VMs MUST have disk.EnableUUID=TRUE in the VMX settings. Without it, Rook cannot stably identify virtual disks across reboots and OSD provisioning silently fails or reassigns wrong devices.
REPLICATED_SIZE_3_OR_EC - For a 3-OSD cluster use replicated size: 3 with failureDomain: host. Never erasure-code a cluster with fewer than dataChunks + codingChunks OSDs on separate hosts.

CAPACITY_HEADROOM_20PCT - Keep ≥20% free capacity at all times. Ceph performance degrades sharply above 80% and enters HEALTH_WARN at 85%, HEALTH_ERR at 95% (nearfull/full thresholds). CRUSH backfill stalls when full.
PG_AUTOSCALER_ON - Enable pg_autoscaler module in every cluster. Manual pg_num management on small clusters leads to HEALTH_WARN 'too few PGs per OSD' or wasted PG overhead.

FSGROUP_IS_DANGEROUS_ON_RWX - Setting fsGroup in a pod spec with a CephFS PVC triggers recursive chown/chmod on every container start. On directories with thousands of files (WordPress uploads) this causes multi-minute ContainerCreating hangs or MDS flood. Use fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch or omit fsGroup entirely.

layer_0_ceph_architecture.description: Core Ceph concepts and Rook operator architecture as they apply to on-premise K8s

truths: Ceph exposes three interfaces on top of RADOS: RBD (block), CephFS (POSIX filesystem via MDS), RGW (S3/Swift object gateway).
All three share the same underlying RADOS cluster and OSD pool storage.
RBD → ReadWriteOnce block device; ideal for MySQL/PostgreSQL, single-pod stateful workloads.
CephFS → ReadWriteMany POSIX filesystem; ideal for shared config, multi-pod legacy apps; requires MDS daemons.
RGW → S3/Swift HTTP gateway; ideal for media, backups, any workload that tolerates eventual consistency and works with S3 SDK; no kernel mount required.
Rook Operator pod watches CephCluster and other CRDs; reconciles desired vs actual state.
Ceph MON pods (3): maintain cluster map and quorum; all metadata operations go through MONs. Must be on separate nodes with anti-affinity.
Ceph MGR pods (1-2): telemetry, dashboard, modules (pg_autoscaler, prometheus, crash). Stateless; safe to restart.
Ceph OSD pods (1 per disk): actual data storage. One OSD = one raw disk (BlueStore). Do not share disks between OSDs.
Ceph MDS pods: required only when CephFilesystem CR exists. Provides active/standby metadata servers.
Ceph RGW pods: required only when CephObjectStore CR exists. HTTP gateway pods; stateless, scalable.
Rook is not in the data path; CSI drivers (csi-rbdplugin, csi-cephfsplugin) handle volume mount/unmount.
CSI provisioner pods handle PVC create/delete; CSI node plugin daemonsets handle mount on each node.
Placement Groups (PGs) are the unit of data distribution across OSDs. Too few → HEALTH_WARN 'too few PGs per OSD'. Too many → RAM overhead on MONs.
Enable pg_autoscaler module (default in Nautilus+). Do not manually set pg_num on pools unless you have >50 OSDs.
Formula for manual sizing: pg_num = (Target PGs per OSD × OSDs × replication_factor) / pool_count. Rule of thumb: 32 PGs per OSD for small clusters.
PG states to understand: active+clean (healthy), active+undersized (insufficient replicas), active+degraded (data at risk), active+remapped (backfilling).
HEALTH_WARN on PGs resolves automatically as OSDs come online or data backfills; do not force-delete PGs.
CRUSH map defines how data is distributed. Default failure domain is 'host' — data replicated across different host nodes.
For a 3-node cluster with failureDomain: host and size: 3, losing 1 host leaves cluster degraded but readable/writable.
ESXi virtual disks all report as HDD device class even if backed by SSDs. Override with deviceClass: ssd in pool spec or use crushDeviceClass in CephCluster.
Custom CRUSH weights can be set with ceph osd crush reweight but Rook may overwrite them on reconcile; prefer per-pool deviceClass.

layer_1_esxi_vmware_specifics.description: Critical ESXi/VMware configuration requirements for Rook Ceph to function correctly

truths: CRITICAL: VMware VMs must have disk.EnableUUID = TRUE in their .vmx file (VM Advanced Settings in vSphere UI). Without this, virtual disks receive non-persistent UUIDs and Rook/Ceph cannot stably identify OSDs across reboots.
Symptom without disk.EnableUUID: OSD pods fail to start silently; osd-prepare jobs complete but no OSD deployment appears; ceph status shows 0 OSDs.
Set via vSphere UI: VM → Edit Settings → VM Options → Advanced → Configuration Parameters → Add Row: disk.EnableUUID = TRUE. Requires VM power-off.
Set via CLI: vmkfstools or govc: govc vm.change -vm <vmname> -e disk.EnableUUID=TRUE
After enabling, verify in guest: ls -la /dev/disk/by-id/ should show scsi-* symlinks with stable UUIDs.
Add a dedicated virtual disk per OSD node for Ceph. Do not use the OS disk or shared VMDK.
Rook requires raw unpartitioned disks with no filesystem. Ensure new VMDKs are provisioned as Thick Provisioned Eager Zeroed for best BlueStore performance.
HP ProLiant DL360 G8 with RAID-1 SSD: present one logical unit per host to the VM. RAID-1 provides hardware redundancy; Ceph replication provides data-level redundancy.
SCSI controller must be VMware Paravirtual (PVSCSI) for production IOPS; do not use LSI Logic SAS.
Disk device filter in CephCluster: use deviceFilter: '^sd[b-z]' to exclude the OS disk /dev/sda.
Virtual disk device class: Ceph detects all ESXi virtual disks as 'hdd'. Override by setting storage.config.deviceClass: ssd in CephCluster spec or use ceph osd crush set-device-class ssd osd.<id>.
Ceph recommends separate public and cluster networks. For small ESXi deployments a single VM network VLAN is acceptable but monitor for bandwidth contention.
MON communication uses port 3300 (v2) and 6789 (v1). OSD communication: ports 6800-7300. RGW: port 80 (ClusterIP).
If host networking is enabled in CephCluster spec, MON endpoints use node IPs instead of ClusterIPs. Prefer ClusterIP (hostNetwork: false) for standard K8s networking.
Jumbo frames (MTU 9000) benefit large OSD data transfers; set on ESXi vSwitch and VM NICs if possible.

layer_2_cephcluster_cr.description: CephCluster CRD configuration patterns for small on-premise clusters (2-6 nodes)

truths: Always set dataDirHostPath: /var/lib/rook — MON data persists across pod restarts. Missing this causes MON restart loops.
mon.count: 3 with allowMultiplePerNode: false is mandatory for quorum safety.
mgr.count: 2 for MGR active/standby failover. mgr-sidecar is lightweight.
storage.useAllNodes: false — explicitly list nodes with storage roles.
storage.useAllDevices: false — use deviceFilter ('^sd[b-z]') to avoid consuming OS disk.
Enable pg_autoscaler: mgr.modules: [{name: pg_autoscaler, enabled: true}].
removeOSDsIfOutAndSafeToRemove: true — auto-cleanup evicted OSD deployments.
MON: requests: {cpu: '1', memory: '4Gi'}. Never set limits on MON — OOM kill destroys quorum.
MGR: requests: {cpu: '1', memory: '2Gi'}. Limits acceptable only on memory at 4Gi.
OSD: requests: {cpu: '2', memory: '4Gi'}. OSD memory auto-tuned by Ceph (osd_memory_target). Do not set CPU limits.
RGW: requests: {cpu: '500m', memory: '1Gi'}. RGW is stateless; limits acceptable.
MDS: requests: {cpu: '1', memory: '4Gi'} in CephFilesystem spec, not CephCluster.
prepareosd jobs need temporary CPU/RAM for BlueStore init: requests: {cpu: '500m', memory: '2Gi'}.
Set priorityClassName: system-node-critical for MON and OSD; system-cluster-critical for MGR.
MON placement must enforce anti-affinity across nodes. Rook sets this by default but verify in small clusters.
OSD placement: taint storage-only nodes with ceph-storage=true:NoSchedule and add tolerations to OSD pods.
RGW placement: spread across 2+ nodes with podAntiAffinity preferredDuringScheduling to prevent single-node failure taking down S3 endpoint.
Label storage nodes: kubectl label node <node> role=storage-node ceph-osd=true

YAML: apiVersion: ceph.rook.io/v1 | kind: CephCluster | metadata: {name: rook-ceph, namespace: rook-ceph} | spec: {cephVersion: {image: 'quay.io/ceph/ceph:v18'}, dataDirHostPath: '/var/lib/rook', mon: {count: 3, allowMultiplePerNode: false}, mgr: {count: 2, modules: [{name: pg_autoscaler, enabled: true}]}, dashboard: {enabled: true, ssl: false}, storage: {useAllNodes: false, useAllDevices: false, deviceFilter: '^sd[b-z]', nodes: [{name: 'node1'}, {name: 'node2'}, {name: 'node3'}]}, resources: {mon: {requests: {cpu: '1', memory: '4Gi'}}, mgr: {requests: {cpu: '1', memory: '2Gi'}}, osd: {requests: {cpu: '2', memory: '4Gi'}}}}

layer_3_rgw_object_storage.description: Ceph RGW (RADOS Gateway) S3-compatible object storage — primary interface for WordPress media sharing

truths: CephObjectStore CR creates RGW daemon deployment + metadata and data pools.
metadataPool: replicated.size: 3 — stores bucket metadata, user info, object index.
dataPool: replicated.size: 3 (small cluster) or erasureCoded: {dataChunks: 2, codingChunks: 1} (≥4-OSD cluster).
gateway.instances: 2 for HA; instances: 1 acceptable for development.
gateway.port: 80 (HTTP); securePort: 443 requires sslCertificateRef pointing to TLS Secret.
preservePoolsOnDelete: true — prevents accidental data loss when CephObjectStore is deleted.
RGW service name pattern: rook-ceph-rgw-<storeName>.rook-ceph.svc.cluster.local:80
CephObjectStoreUser CR creates an RGW user and stores AccessKey + SecretKey in a K8s Secret named rook-ceph-object-user-<store>-<username>.
User capabilities (caps) control admin operations: capabilities: {user: 'read', bucket: 'read write', usage: 'read', metadata: 'read write', zone: 'read'}.
For WordPress: create one user per logical tenant group. Single shared user across all WP pods is simplest.
Max-buckets quota: maxBuckets controls how many buckets the user may own. Default 1000.
Secret format: data.AccessKey (base64), data.SecretKey (base64). Mount as env vars in WordPress pod.
Cross-namespace access: copy Secret to WordPress namespace with kubectl or use ExternalSecret operator.
Buckets can be created via ObjectBucketClaim (OBC) CRD (auto-provisioned) or via radosgw-admin / mc directly.
OBC creates a bucket + a ConfigMap (endpoint, bucket name) + a Secret (access/secret keys) in same namespace.
For shared multi-deployment access, create bucket manually and distribute credentials; OBC per-deployment creates isolated buckets.
radosgw-admin bucket create --bucket=wp-media --uid=wp-user
radosgw-admin bucket stats --bucket=wp-media — shows object count, size, placement.
Bucket lifecycle policy: set via S3 API (boto3/aws-cli) on RGW endpoint for automatic deletion of old objects.
Bucket policy JSON for public-read: {Statement: [{Effect: Allow, Principal: *, Action: s3:GetObject, Resource: arn:aws:s3:::wp-media/*}]}
RGW bucket policies and ACLs are independent. Policy wins if both set. Prefer bucket policies over per-object ACLs for consistency.
Default RGW service type is ClusterIP — accessible only within cluster.
For WordPress pods in same cluster: use ClusterIP URL http://rook-ceph-rgw-my-store.rook-ceph.svc.cluster.local:80
For nginx CDN proxy (in-cluster): nginx backend = same ClusterIP URL; CDN domain is set in S3 plugin as custom delivery domain.
For external access: create NodePort Service (not modifying the default ClusterIP) or add Ingress pointing to the RGW Service.
Ingress annotation nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: '0' is mandatory for large media uploads.
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-request-buffering: 'off' prevents timeouts on large object PUT requests.
WordPress media (thumbnails, compressed images) are small files (2KB–2MB). RGW performs well for these but latency per-object matters more than throughput.
rgw_thread_pool_size: increase from default 512 to 1024 in ceph.conf for high-concurrency WordPress sites.
rgw_cache_lru_size: default 10000. Increase to 50000 for media-heavy workloads.
Use nginx proxy_cache in front of RGW to cache GET requests for static media: proxy_cache_valid 200 7d; proxy_cache_use_stale error timeout updating.
Disable rgw_dynamic_resharding for small buckets with < 100K objects to reduce metadata overhead.
BlueStore compression (snappy) on data pool reduces storage but adds CPU overhead; evaluate on HP G8 RAID-SSD hardware.
Run all radosgw-admin commands from rook-ceph-tools pod: kubectl exec -n rook-ceph deploy/rook-ceph-tools -- radosgw-admin <cmd>
Create user: radosgw-admin user create --uid=wp-shared --display-name='WordPress Shared' --email=admin@example.com
Get credentials: radosgw-admin user info --uid=wp-shared | jq '.keys[0]'
Create bucket: radosgw-admin bucket create --bucket=wp-media --uid=wp-shared
Bucket stats: radosgw-admin bucket stats --bucket=wp-media
List buckets: radosgw-admin bucket list
List objects: radosgw-admin bucket list --bucket=wp-media
Set quota: radosgw-admin quota set --quota-scope=bucket --bucket=wp-media --max-size=100G
Enable quota: radosgw-admin quota enable --quota-scope=bucket --bucket=wp-media
Orphan cleanup: radosgw-admin orphans find --pool=.rgw.data.root --job-id=job1 (finds leaked objects)

layer_4_wordpress_s3_integration.description: WordPress-specific configuration for media offload to Ceph RGW S3

truths: WP Offload Media (AS3CF) does NOT natively support custom S3 endpoints — it requires the 'WP Offload Media Tweaks' companion plugin to register the as3cf_aws_s3_client_args filter.

In WP Offload Media Tweaks class, add: function ceph_s3_client_args($args) { $args['endpoint'] = 'http://rook-ceph-rgw-my-store.rook-ceph.svc.cluster.local'; $args['use_path_style_endpoint'] = true; return $args; } add_filter('as3cf_aws_s3_client_args', [$this, 'ceph_s3_client_args']);
use_path_style_endpoint: true is required for Ceph RGW. RGW does not support virtual-hosted-style bucket URLs by default.
Also add filter to fix URL domain: add_filter('as3cf_aws_s3_url_domain', function($domain, $bucket, $region, $expires, $args) { return 'cdn.vikka.ua/files/wp/' . $bucket; }, 10, 5);

AS3CF_SETTINGS in wp-config.php: define('AS3CF_SETTINGS', serialize(['provider' => 'aws', 'access-key-id' => 'KEYID', 'secret-access-key' => 'SECRET', 'bucket' => 'wp-media', 'region' => 'default', 'copy-to-s3' => true, 'serve-from-s3' => true, 'enable-object-prefix' => true, 'object-prefix' => 'wp-content/uploads/', 'remove-local-file' => false]));
Advanced Media Offloader (ADVMO) natively supports any S3-compatible endpoint via its 'MinIO' provider option — better choice than WP Offload Media for Ceph RGW.

wp-config.php defines: define('ADVMO_MINIO_KEY', 'ACCESS_KEY'); define('ADVMO_MINIO_SECRET', 'SECRET_KEY'); define('ADVMO_MINIO_BUCKET', 'wp-media'); define('ADVMO_MINIO_ENDPOINT', 'http://rook-ceph-rgw-my-store.rook-ceph.svc.cluster.local'); define('ADVMO_MINIO_PATH_STYLE_ENDPOINT', true); define('ADVMO_MINIO_DOMAIN', 'https://cdn.vikka.ua'); define('ADVMO_MINIO_REGION', 'default');
ADVMO does not modify database URLs — it dynamically rewrites wp_get_attachment_url() output at runtime. All stored DB URLs remain as wp-content/uploads/... paths; CDN URLs are generated on the fly.
This is the correct pattern for shared DB multi-pod setups: each pod reads the local-path URL from DB, ADVMO rewrites to CDN URL transparently.
WP-CLI bulk offload: wp advmo offload --batch=100 (requires ADVMO CLI add-on)
Pattern: All WordPress pods share MySQL DB with identical wp_posts / wp_postmeta / wp_attachments tables. Media metadata (filenames, sizes, paths) is consistent across pods.
All pods point to the SAME RGW bucket with the SAME credentials. Pod A uploads → object lands in RGW → Pod B reads same RGW URL immediately.
S3 plugin MUST be configured with the same bucket, same prefix, and same CDN domain on all pods. Divergent configs cause URL mismatch.
K8s Secret (from CephObjectStoreUser) is mounted as env vars in all WordPress Deployments: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, S3_BUCKET_NAME, S3_ENDPOINT_URL.
If pods are in different namespaces, copy the RGW credentials Secret to each namespace or use a ClusterSecret controller.

Upload flow: user uploads via WP admin → file written to /wp-content/uploads/ locally → ADVMO copies to RGW → (optionally) local file deleted. On next page load, ADVMO rewrites attachment URL to CDN domain.
The S3 plugin does NOT update database URLs; it rewrites at PHP runtime. This is safe for shared DB — no migration needed when adding a new pod.
Initial migration from existing wp-content/uploads/ to RGW bucket:
Step 1 — Install ADVMO/AS3CF on all pods with RGW credentials.
Step 2 — Use mc mirror to sync existing files: mc mirror ./wp-content/uploads/ myrook/wp-media/wp-content/uploads/
Step 3 — Run bulk offload via WP-CLI (marks DB metadata as offloaded): wp advmo offload --all
Step 4 — Verify: spot-check attachment URLs in WP admin → Media Library; confirm CDN domain appears.
Step 5 — Enable 'Remove local files after offload' to free container storage.
mc alias set myrook http://rook-ceph-rgw-my-store.rook-ceph.svc.cluster.local ACCESSKEY SECRETKEY
mc ls myrook/wp-media — verify object count matches wp-content/uploads/ file count.
nginx acts as CDN proxy: all media requests to cdn.vikka.ua/files/wp/ are proxied to RGW bucket.

nginx.conf location block: location /files/wp/ { proxy_pass http://rook-ceph-rgw-my-store.rook-ceph.svc.cluster.local/wp-media/wp-content/uploads/; proxy_cache wp_media_cache; proxy_cache_valid 200 7d; proxy_cache_use_stale error timeout updating; proxy_cache_lock on; add_header X-Cache-Status $upstream_cache_status; }
proxy_cache_path /var/cache/nginx/wp_media levels=1:2 keys_zone=wp_media_cache:10m max_size=20g inactive=30d;
Set client_max_body_size 256m in nginx to allow large media uploads.
Cache invalidation: mc rm myrook/wp-media/<path> + nginx cache purge (ngx_cache_purge module) or just let TTL expire.
For geo-replication: mc mirror --watch myrook/wp-media remoterook/wp-media runs continuous sync between two RGW endpoints.

layer_5_cephfs.description: CephFS filesystem storage — ReadWriteMany workloads, pitfalls, and when to prefer RGW instead

truths: CephFS is appropriate for: multi-pod shared config files, shared code directories, legacy apps that require POSIX filesystem semantics (rename, hard links, directory listing).
CephFS is NOT appropriate for: high-throughput media serving (latency per-request too high vs RGW with nginx cache), databases (use RBD), pure object workloads (use RGW).
For WordPress: CephFS RWX can replace shared NFS for wp-content/plugins/ and wp-content/themes/ sync — but NOT for uploads/ (use RGW instead).
CephFS PVCs in RWX mode can be shared across pods in the SAME namespace directly. Cross-namespace sharing requires static PV clone pattern (copy PV, create PVC pointing to it).
CRITICAL: Setting fsGroup in a pod's securityContext when a CephFS volume is mounted triggers Kubernetes to recursively chown/chmod ALL files in the volume on every container start.
With thousands of WordPress media files, this causes pods to hang in ContainerCreating for minutes or indefinitely, flooding MDS with setxattr syscalls.
Fix: set securityContext.fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch — kubelet only changes ownership if root directory ownership doesn't match. This avoids recursive walk.
Alternative: omit fsGroup entirely and set file permissions in the container via initContainer or dockerfile.
SELinux relabeling causes the same symptom (recursive setxattr). Disable SELinux on CephFS mount nodes or use CSI_FORCE_CEPHFS_KERNEL_CLIENT: false to switch to FUSE client.
CephFilesystem CR: metadata pool (replicated size 3) + one or more data pools (replicated size 3).
metadataServer.activeCount: 1 for small clusters; activeStandby: true for fast failover.
MDS resources in CephFilesystem spec (not CephCluster): resources: {requests: {cpu: '1', memory: '4Gi'}}.
StorageClass: provisioner: rook-ceph.cephfs.csi.ceph.com | parameters: {fsName: myfs, pool: myfs-data0, csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-name: rook-csi-cephfs-provisioner}.
CephFS quotas require kernel ≥ 4.17. On Ubuntu 22.04 with kernel 5.15 quotas work natively.
CephFilesystemSubVolumeGroup CRD: creates an isolated namespace within the filesystem for tenant separation — OSDs shared, but namespaces isolated.

layer_6_rbd_block_storage.description: Ceph RBD block storage for databases and single-pod workloads

truths: RBD = ReadWriteOnce. One PVC can only be mounted on one node at a time. Suitable for: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Redis, single-replica Deployments or StatefulSets.
RBD PVCs can expand online in Rook Ceph (allowVolumeExpansion: true in StorageClass). No unmount required.
RBD StorageClass: provisioner: rook-ceph.rbd.csi.ceph.com | parameters: {pool: replicapool, imageFeatures: layering}.
imageFeatures: layering is required for broad kernel compatibility. Deep-features (exclusive-lock, object-map, fast-diff) improve performance on modern kernels.
For MySQL: use xfs filesystem in RBD PVC (volumeMode: Filesystem, fsType: xfs in StorageClass). XFS handles MySQL write patterns better than ext4.
BlueStore default RocksDB WAL and DB are co-located on OSD disk. For dedicated RAID-SSD OSDs on HP G8, no separate WAL/DB device needed.
OSD memory target: set osd_memory_target: 4294967296 (4GiB) per OSD in rook-config-override ConfigMap for consistent performance.
For MySQL workloads: ceph osd pool set replicapool compression_mode none (disable compression for latency-sensitive block I/O).
RBD mirroring: for cross-cluster DR, configure CephRBDMirror CR with token-based replication. Not needed for single on-premise cluster.

layer_7_health_warn_triage.description: Interpreting and resolving common Ceph HEALTH_WARN and HEALTH_ERR states

truths: HEALTH_WARN clock skew detected: NTP not synced across K8s nodes. Fix: timedatectl status on all nodes; ensure chronyd/ntpd is running.
HEALTH_WARN too few PGs per OSD: pg_autoscaler disabled or pg_num not autoscaled yet. Enable autoscaler: ceph mgr module enable pg_autoscaler; ceph osd pool set <pool> pg_autoscale_mode on
HEALTH_WARN nearfull OSDs: OSDs approaching 85% capacity. Add OSDs or delete data immediately. Ceph will stop writes at 95% (osd_full_ratio).
HEALTH_WARN mon clock skew: ntpd issue. Also check mon_clock_drift_allowed config.
HEALTH_WARN degraded data redundancy X/Y objects degraded: Normal during OSD add/remove/rebalance. Becomes HEALTH_ERR if degraded > 0 and OSD is down (insufficient replicas).
HEALTH_WARN 1 OSDs or CRUSH nodes have {NOUP,NODOWN,NOIN,NOOUT} flags: Manual flags set. Remove with: ceph osd unset noup (etc.)
HEALTH_ERR 1 mon is down: Quorum at risk. One MON pod crashed. Check pod logs. Restart or failover MON.
HEALTH_ERR full OSDs: Writes blocked. Emergency: ceph osd set nofull (temporarily); delete data or add OSDs urgently.
ceph status — overall health, services, data summary
ceph health detail — verbose HEALTH_WARN/ERR explanations
ceph osd tree — CRUSH hierarchy, OSD weights and states
ceph osd df — per-OSD disk usage and PG count
ceph df — pool-level usage statistics
ceph pg dump_stuck — show stuck PGs (inactive, unclean, stale)
ceph pg stat — PG count by state
ceph osd perf — per-OSD latency (read/write commit lat)
ceph tell osd.* config show — dump running config of all OSDs
ceph log last 100 — recent cluster log events
kubectl logs -n rook-ceph -l app=rook-ceph-mon -c mon — MON pod logs
kubectl logs -n rook-ceph rook-ceph-operator-<pod> — Operator reconcile logs

layer_8_csi_debugging.description: Debugging CSI mount failures for RBD and CephFS PVCs

truths: PVC stays Pending → provisioner not responding. Check csi-rbdplugin-provisioner or csi-cephfsplugin-provisioner pod logs.
kubectl logs -n rook-ceph deploy/csi-rbdplugin-provisioner -c csi-provisioner — external-provisioner errors.
kubectl logs -n rook-ceph deploy/csi-rbdplugin-provisioner -c csi-rbdplugin — CSI RBD driver errors.
Common cause: MON connectivity failure. Verify: kubectl exec -n rook-ceph deploy/rook-ceph-tools -- ceph -s
Common cause: wrong StorageClass provisioner string. Must match operator namespace: rook-ceph.rbd.csi.ceph.com
Common cause: CSI secrets missing (rook-csi-rbd-provisioner, rook-csi-cephfs-provisioner). Check they exist in rook-ceph namespace.
Pod stuck ContainerCreating with FailedMount event → CSI node plugin not running on that node.
Check csi-rbdplugin DaemonSet: kubectl get pods -n rook-ceph -l app=csi-rbdplugin -o wide — must have Running pod on node where app pod is scheduled.
Restart stuck CSI node plugin: kubectl delete pod -n rook-ceph <csi-rbdplugin-xxxxx>
CephFS pod hanging in ContainerCreating: likely fsGroup recursive chown (see fsgroup_pitfall) or MDS unavailable.
Check MDS: ceph mds stat — should show 1 active MDS. If no active MDS, check rook-ceph-mds-* pod logs.
NetworkPolicy blocking CSI → MON: ensure rook-ceph namespace has no NetworkPolicy blocking port 3300/6789 from worker nodes.

layer_9_operational_commands.description: Day-2 operations: OSD management, bucket operations, benchmarking

truths: Add OSD: attach new disk to node, deviceFilter matches it → Rook auto-provisions OSD. Verify: watch kubectl get pods -n rook-ceph -l app=rook-ceph-osd.
Remove OSD gracefully: ceph osd out osd.<ID> → wait for rebalance → kubectl apply -f osd-purge.yaml (set OSD-IDs in spec) → wipe disk.
Replace failed OSD: ceph osd out osd.<ID>; kubectl delete deploy rook-ceph-osd-<N>-*; replace physical/virtual disk; let Rook auto-reprovision.
Check OSD status: ceph osd status — shows per-OSD state, used/available, ops.
Force OSD down: ceph osd down osd.<ID> (for testing failover).
Stop Rook operator during manual OSD work: kubectl scale deploy -n rook-ceph rook-ceph-operator --replicas=0 (restart after: --replicas=1).
mc alias set myrook http://rook-ceph-rgw-my-store.rook-ceph.svc.cluster.local ACCESSKEY SECRETKEY
mc ls myrook/ — list buckets
mc ls myrook/wp-media/ — list objects
mc cp ./image.jpg myrook/wp-media/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/image.jpg — upload single file
mc mirror ./wp-content/uploads/ myrook/wp-media/wp-content/uploads/ — one-time sync (local → bucket)
mc mirror --watch ./wp-content/uploads/ myrook/wp-media/ — continuous sync (use for warm standby)
mc mirror --remove myrook/source/ myrook/dest/ — sync between two RGW buckets (cross-cluster geo-replication)
mc rm --recursive --force myrook/wp-media/wp-content/uploads/2020/ — delete old year's uploads
mc stat myrook/wp-media/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/image.jpg — check object metadata
mc du myrook/wp-media/ — bucket disk usage summary
rados bench (block-level, OSD pool): kubectl exec -n rook-ceph deploy/rook-ceph-tools -- rados bench -p replicapool 60 write --no-cleanup
rados bench read: kubectl exec -n rook-ceph deploy/rook-ceph-tools -- rados bench -p replicapool 60 seq
S3 throughput via s3-benchmark: docker run -e endpoint=http://RGW_IP:80 -e accessKey=KEY -e secretKey=SECRET minio/s3-benchmark
fio on RBD PVC: kubectl exec <db-pod> -- fio --name=rbd-test --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --numjobs=4 --size=1G --runtime=60 --ioengine=libaio --direct=1
Latency check: ceph osd perf | sort -k3 -n | tail -5 — shows slowest OSDs by apply latency.
Ceph dashboard runs in MGR pod. Expose: kubectl port-forward -n rook-ceph svc/rook-ceph-mgr-dashboard 7000:7000
Get admin password: kubectl get secret -n rook-ceph rook-ceph-dashboard-password -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
Username: admin. Default port: 8443 (HTTPS) or 7000 (HTTP, if dashboard.ssl: false in CephCluster).
To expose via Ingress: create Ingress pointing to Service rook-ceph-mgr-dashboard on port 7000.
Dashboard shows: cluster health, OSD tree, pool usage, RGW endpoints, active ops, performance graphs.

layer_10_anti_patterns.description: Common mistakes that cause silent failures, data loss, or performance degradation

truths: ANTI-PATTERN: Missing disk.EnableUUID on ESXi VMs → OSD provisioning silently fails. Fix: enable in VMX config before provisioning cluster.
ANTI-PATTERN: Using OS disk for OSD (no deviceFilter) → OS partition consumed, node becomes unbootable. Fix: always set deviceFilter: '^sd[b-z]'.
ANTI-PATTERN: Setting CPU Limits on MON/OSD → CPU throttling causes MON quorum timeout, OSD slow ops, HEALTH_WARN. Fix: use Requests only, never Limits.
ANTI-PATTERN: Setting Memory Limits on MON → OOM kill destroys quorum. Fix: no memory limits on MONs.
ANTI-PATTERN: Single OSD in production (replicated size 1) → no redundancy; any OSD failure = data loss. Fix: minimum 3 OSDs across 3 nodes with size: 3.
ANTI-PATTERN: Two MONs only → quorum fails if either MON crashes. Fix: always 3 MONs.
ANTI-PATTERN: fsGroup on CephFS RWX pods with many files → recursive chown causes ContainerCreating timeout. Fix: fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch or omit fsGroup.
ANTI-PATTERN: Using virtual-hosted-style S3 URLs with Ceph RGW without configuration → 403 or DNS resolution failure. Fix: use_path_style_endpoint: true in S3 client.
ANTI-PATTERN: WP Offload Media without Tweaks plugin pointing to AWS endpoint → all S3 calls hit amazonaws.com. Fix: register as3cf_aws_s3_client_args filter with custom endpoint.
ANTI-PATTERN: Separate S3 buckets per WordPress pod for shared media → pods see different media sets. Fix: one shared bucket, all pods use same credentials and prefix.
ANTI-PATTERN: Ceph pool at >80% capacity → performance cliff, HEALTH_WARN nearfull, CRUSH backfill stalls. Fix: monitor with ceph df; keep ≤80% used.
ANTI-PATTERN: Erasure coding with fewer OSDs than dataChunks + codingChunks on separate hosts → PGs stuck undersized. Fix: replicated size 3 for small clusters.
ANTI-PATTERN: Missing dataDirHostPath in CephCluster CR → MONs lose data on pod restart, perpetual reconcile loop. Fix: dataDirHostPath: /var/lib/rook.
ANTI-PATTERN: Leaving stale OSD Deployments after disk removal → Rook may reassign them to new disks incorrectly. Fix: use osd-purge Job and remove from CR.
ANTI-PATTERN: RGW bucket ACLs and bucket policies both set with conflicting rules → policy wins, ACL ignored. Fix: use only bucket policy JSON for access control.
ANTI-PATTERN: nginx proxy_body_size default (1MB) with large media uploads → 413 Request Entity Too Large. Fix: client_max_body_size 256m in nginx.

ceph_object_store.yaml:
apiVersion: ceph.rook.io/v1
kind: CephObjectStore
metadata:
  name: my-store
  namespace: rook-ceph
spec:
  metadataPool:
    failureDomain: host
    replicated:
      size: 3
  dataPool:
    failureDomain: host
    replicated:
      size: 3
    parameters:
      compression_mode: passive
  preservePoolsOnDelete: true
  gateway:
    port: 80
    instances: 2
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: '500m'
        memory: '1Gi'
    placement:
      podAntiAffinity:
        preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - weight: 100
            podAffinityTerm:
              labelSelector:
                matchExpressions:
                  - key: app
                    operator: In
                    values: [rook-ceph-rgw]
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname

storage_interface_selection.wordpress_media_shared: RGW (S3) — multiple pods, S3 plugin (ADVMO), CDN fronting
storage_interface_selection.wordpress_plugins_themes_shared: CephFS RWX — POSIX required, set fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch
storage_interface_selection.wordpress_uploads_single_pod: RBD RWO — acceptable if pods never scale > 1
storage_interface_selection.backup_store: RGW (S3) — Velero uses S3 API natively
storage_interface_selection.high_iops_database: RBD — BlueStore + RAID-SSD OSD, no compression

when_rgw_beats_cephfs: Multiple pods across multiple nodes need write access (RGW has no fsGroup issue)
Media files accessed via CDN (nginx can cache S3 GET responses; not CephFS mounts)
No POSIX semantics needed (no rename, no hardlinks, no directory listing in app code)
Media files stored with absolute CDN URLs in DB (perfect for S3 plugin URL rewrite)
Bucket lifecycle policies needed for automatic cleanup
when_cephfs_beats_rgw: Legacy app requires POSIX filesystem (rename, flock, hard links)
App cannot use S3 SDK and requires mounted filesystem path
Very small number of frequently-updated shared config files
Direct NFS-style access needed from multiple pods

known_limitations: ESXi RAID-1 virtual disk presents as single block device to OS; Ceph adds software replication on top — effective data written is 3× raw (3 Ceph replicas × 1 RAID-1 mirror). Account for this in capacity planning.
Ceph RGW does not support virtual-hosted-style bucket URLs without custom DNS wildcard setup. Always use path-style (bucket-in-path) for self-hosted RGW.
WP Offload Media (AS3CF) requires the 'Tweaks' companion plugin for custom S3 endpoints; Advanced Media Offloader (ADVMO) supports custom endpoints natively — prefer ADVMO for Ceph RGW.
CephFS cross-namespace PVC sharing requires manual static PV clone pattern; Rook does not automate this.
ESXi virtual disks are always classified as 'hdd' device class; set crushDeviceClass: ssd manually in pools or OSD config to place data on correct CRUSH class.
Rook 1.x does not support in-place disk replacement; must use out-then-in OSD replacement workflow.
RGW multisite replication (for geo-DR) requires CephObjectZone/CephObjectZoneGroup CRDs; single-zone is sufficient for single-datacenter deployments.
Ceph pg_autoscaler can produce HEALTH_WARN 'large skew in PG count' on mixed-workload clusters; acknowledge with: ceph health mute POOL_PG_NUM_NOT_POWER_OF_TWO
